A Sri Lankan soldier was seen moving through Mullaittivu, which had previously served as the Tamil rebels’ military headquarters.

A relief worker told CNN on Sunday that more than 200 civilians, including at least 30 children, had been wounded during the previous three days of combat. The worker, who asked not to be named because of concerns that relief operations could be put at risk, said that figure was “the absolute minimum” number of injured people.

Sri Lankan authorities have accused aid groups and international media outlets of overstating civilian casualty figures. Dr. Palitha Kohona, the country’s secretary of foreign affairs, told CNN that it appeared “convenient for certain agencies” to inflate the numbers in order to portray the situation publicly as a humanitarian crisis.

On Sunday, Defense Secretary Gotabaya Rajapaksa said Sri Lanka would “continue with the military offensive until we liberate the remaining area under LTTE control,” according to the country’s state-run news agency. The LTTE is the rebel organization also known as the Tamil Tigers.

A United Nations spokesman said Saturday that a small number of U.N. personnel were working continuously to assist the rising number of children caught in the fighting. James Elder, the spokesman, told CNN that children as young as 4 months old were being treated at local hospitals for shrapnel wounds and other injuries caused by the war.

Elder said the fighting was extremely intense in a limited area where children and other civilians remained. He added that the area affected by the conflict was getting smaller while the violence was increasing.

According to Elder, U.N. aid workers on Thursday evacuated 50 children in critical condition and 105 adults. He said relief workers were attempting to remove as many people from the area as possible.

Humanitarian organizations estimate that up to 250,000 civilians without protection are trapped in the conflict zone.

Sri Lankan President Mahinda Rajapaksa has pledged to provide safe passage for civilians who are stuck there and has called on the Tamil Tigers to make the same commitment. In a statement posted on the government’s Web site, Rajapaksa said authorities had established a civilian safe zone and that security forces had announced its coordinates.

He also accused the Tamil Tiger organization of abusing the designated safe area by positioning heavy artillery inside it and using the location to launch attacks on security forces while also killing civilians indiscriminately.

Elder described conditions for civilians in the war zone as “nightmarish.” He said the crisis was being worsened by a developing shortage of humanitarian supplies and reduced access to clean water, sanitation, and food.

Also on Sunday, Sri Lankan troops captured an important rebel stronghold during an unexpected assault deep inside Tamil-held territory. The government-run news agency reported that soldiers crossed a lagoon and entered Mullaittivu before meeting strong resistance from Tamil fighters.

The Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam, or LTTE, commonly referred to as the Tamil Tigers, have been waging a campaign since 1983 for a separate homeland for Sri Lanka’s ethnic Tamil minority. The civil war has killed more than 70,000 people.

**Artillery shells hit hospital in Sri Lanka war zone, aid officials say**

*MULLAITTIVU, Sri Lanka* — Artillery shells struck a hospital in Sri Lanka’s northern war zone as government forces battled Tamil Tiger rebels, killing and wounding civilians already trapped by weeks of fighting, aid and U.N. officials said.

The attack occurred in Mullaittivu district, where tens of thousands of civilians were caught between advancing Sri Lankan troops and the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam, or LTTE. Medical workers and humanitarian officials said shells landed on or near a functioning hospital treating war wounded, including women and children.

Casualty figures were difficult to verify because access to the conflict zone was severely restricted. Local medical officials reported multiple civilian deaths and dozens of injuries, while aid agencies warned that the number could rise because hospitals in the area were overwhelmed and short of medicine, staff and basic supplies.

The United Nations expressed deep concern over the shelling and renewed calls for both sides to protect civilians and respect international humanitarian law. U.N. officials said hospitals and medical workers must never be targeted and urged a pause in the fighting to allow civilians to leave the combat zone safely.

Humanitarian agencies also warned that civilians had little access to food, clean water or emergency care. Many families had fled repeatedly as the front lines shifted, taking shelter in makeshift bunkers and crowded camps.

Sri Lanka’s government denied deliberately targeting civilians or medical facilities, saying its military was conducting operations against LTTE positions and accusing the rebels of using civilians as human shields. Officials said troops were taking precautions to avoid civilian casualties and blamed the Tigers for preventing people from escaping the war zone.

The LTTE, which had fought for decades to create a separate Tamil homeland in northern and eastern Sri Lanka, accused government forces of indiscriminate shelling. The government rejected that charge and said it was in the final stages of defeating the rebel group.

Independent confirmation of the hospital strike was not immediately possible because journalists and most international aid workers were barred from the area. The shelling added to mounting international pressure on both sides as the civilian toll of the conflict continued to grow.

**BREAKING NEWS REPORT — January 2009**

**Sri Lankan Civilians Trapped as Army Advances on LTTE Stronghold in Mullaittivu**

*MULLAITTIVU DISTRICT, Sri Lanka — January 2009*  

Tens of thousands of civilians, including large numbers of children, are trapped in a rapidly shrinking war zone in northeastern Sri Lanka as government forces press a major offensive against the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam, or LTTE, in Mullaittivu District.

The Sri Lankan army says it is closing in on the rebels’ remaining positions after months of advances across the north, capturing key LTTE-held towns and pushing the insurgent group toward a narrow coastal strip. Military officials describe the operation as the final phase of a long campaign to defeat the LTTE, which has fought for decades to establish a separate Tamil state.

But as the front lines move deeper into Mullaittivu, aid agencies and human rights groups warn that civilians are caught between the advancing army and the retreating Tigers, with limited access to food, clean water, medical care, and safe passage.

### Children Among Those at Greatest Risk

Reports from the conflict zone indicate that families are sheltering in makeshift bunkers, schools, churches, and overcrowded temporary camps as shelling and fighting intensify. Children are believed to be suffering from injuries, malnutrition, dehydration, and severe trauma.

Humanitarian workers say many children have been displaced multiple times as their families flee from one village to another. Some have been separated from parents during chaotic movements of civilians. Hospitals and medical points in the area are reportedly struggling to treat the wounded with dwindling supplies.

Because independent journalists and many international aid agencies have limited access to the battlefield, exact casualty figures are difficult to verify. However, humanitarian sources say the number of people at risk is substantial, and conditions are deteriorating rapidly.

### Government Declares “Safe Zone,” But Fears Persist

The Sri Lankan government has announced a designated “safe zone” for civilians and has called on people in rebel-held areas to move there. Officials say the army is taking precautions to avoid civilian casualties and accuse the LTTE of using civilians as human shields.

The LTTE has denied some of those accusations, but it has long faced allegations from human rights groups of preventing civilians from leaving areas under its control and recruiting children into its forces. The group has also been accused of positioning military assets close to civilian concentrations.

Aid groups are urging both sides to respect international humanitarian law, allow civilians to move freely, and ensure the wounded can receive treatment.

### A Shrinking Battlefield

The latest fighting follows a series of major government victories. Earlier this month, Sri Lankan forces captured Kilinochchi, the LTTE’s administrative capital, dealing a symbolic and strategic blow to the rebels. The army has since moved eastward toward Mullaittivu, the LTTE’s last major stronghold.

Military commanders say troops are advancing from multiple directions and have seized rebel bases, weapons stores, and defensive positions. The LTTE, once one of the world’s most powerful insurgent movements, is now believed to be confined to a much smaller area along the northeastern coast.

Analysts say the rebels may continue to fight using guerrilla tactics, but the loss of territory has severely weakened their conventional military capability.

### Humanitarian Crisis Deepens

The United Nations and international organizations have warned of a growing humanitarian emergency. Civilians trapped in the conflict zone face shortages of rice, medicine, fuel, and clean drinking water. Movement out of LTTE-held areas remains dangerous and uncertain.

Doctors and local officials have reported treating civilians wounded by artillery, gunfire, and aerial attacks, though verification remains difficult due to restricted access. The government has rejected claims that it is targeting civilians and says its operations are directed at LTTE combatants.

Families attempting to flee government-designated combat areas often face long journeys through mined terrain, lagoon crossings, and front-line fire. Those who reach government-controlled territory are being screened by security forces and sent to displacement camps, where conditions are also under strain.

### Calls for a Pause in Fighting

International pressure is mounting for a humanitarian pause to allow civilians to leave and aid to enter. Human rights organizations are calling for independent monitoring, medical evacuations, and guaranteed protection for noncombatants.

Sri Lankan authorities, however, insist they are close to ending the war and have signaled they do not intend to halt the offensive. The government argues that a pause could allow the LTTE to regroup.

For civilians in Mullaittivu, the immediate concern is survival. With the army advancing, the LTTE retreating, and the battlefield contracting, families have fewer places to go.

### Background: Decades of War

Sri Lanka’s civil war began in 1983, rooted in ethnic tensions between the Sinhalese-majority government and Tamil minority communities. The LTTE emerged as the dominant Tamil militant group, using conventional warfare, suicide bombings, assassinations, and naval attacks in its campaign for an independent Tamil homeland.

The war has killed tens of thousands of people and displaced many more. Previous cease-fires collapsed amid renewed violence, and the government launched its most aggressive northern offensive after formally withdrawing from a cease-fire agreement in 2008.

Now, as fighting reaches Mullaittivu, the war appears to be nearing a decisive military conclusion — but at potentially devastating cost to civilians trapped in the final combat zone.

**Sri Lankan troops seize Mullaittivu as fears grow for civilians trapped in war zone**

*Colombo, Sri Lanka* — Sri Lankan government forces captured the northern town of Mullaittivu, the Tamil Tigers’ last major urban stronghold, in a major battlefield victory that officials said brought the island’s long civil war closer to an end. But as troops advanced deeper into rebel-held territory, humanitarian agencies warned that hundreds of thousands of civilians were trapped in shrinking conflict zones with dwindling access to food, medicine and safe shelter.

The fall of Mullaittivu, a coastal town that had long served as a key base for the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam, or LTTE, marked one of the most significant blows to the separatist movement in years. Sri Lankan military officials said troops entered the town after weeks of intense fighting and were consolidating control while pushing toward remaining rebel positions in the surrounding jungle and coastal areas.

“This is a decisive victory,” government officials said, describing the capture as evidence that the LTTE’s conventional fighting capability was collapsing. State media broadcast images of soldiers raising the Sri Lankan flag and moving through streets and damaged buildings in the former rebel-held town.

Mullaittivu had symbolic and strategic importance for the Tigers, who had controlled large parts of Sri Lanka’s north and east during different stages of the 25-year conflict. The LTTE used the area as a military hub and, according to the government, as a base for naval operations by its “Sea Tigers” wing.

The rebel group, which fought for an independent Tamil homeland in the north and east of the majority-Sinhalese country, did not immediately confirm the loss. In recent months, however, the Tigers had suffered a string of setbacks, including the loss of Kilinochchi, their de facto political capital.

While the government hailed the advance, aid organizations and international officials expressed mounting alarm over the fate of civilians caught between the two sides. Humanitarian groups said large numbers of people had been displaced repeatedly by the fighting and were now confined to a rapidly narrowing area with little ability to escape.

Estimates of the number of trapped civilians varied widely, but aid agencies and local officials warned that the figure could be in the hundreds of thousands. Many were believed to be sheltering in makeshift camps, schools, churches and open ground, with limited access to clean water, medical care and basic supplies.

The United Nations and international relief agencies have called for both sides to protect civilians and allow safe passage out of the combat zone. They have also urged greater humanitarian access, saying the intensifying offensive has made it increasingly difficult to assess casualties or deliver aid.

The Sri Lankan government accused the LTTE of preventing civilians from leaving areas under its control and using them as human shields, a charge the Tigers have repeatedly denied. Human rights organizations have also urged the military to avoid shelling populated areas and to ensure that civilians who flee are treated lawfully and humanely.

Hospitals in the north were reported to be overwhelmed, with shortages of medicine, surgical supplies and staff. Communications with the conflict zone remained limited, and independent verification of battlefield claims and casualty figures was difficult because journalists and most aid workers had restricted access to the area.

For President Mahinda Rajapaksa’s government, the capture of Mullaittivu was presented as a turning point in its campaign to defeat the LTTE militarily. The administration had withdrawn from a faltering ceasefire and pursued an all-out offensive, arguing that only the destruction of the Tigers’ armed wing could end decades of suicide bombings, assassinations and territorial warfare.

But critics warned that a military victory alone would not resolve the ethnic grievances that fueled the conflict. Tamil political leaders and international observers said the government would need to address questions of minority rights, devolution of power, accountability and reconciliation if it hoped to secure a lasting peace.

The war has killed tens of thousands of people since it erupted in the early 1980s. It has also displaced large communities and left deep scars across the island.

As government troops pressed beyond Mullaittivu, the central question shifted from whether the Tigers could hold territory to what would happen to the civilians still trapped in their remaining enclave. Aid workers warned that without urgent action to create safe routes and deliver relief, the final phase of the war could bring a severe humanitarian crisis even as the government celebrated one of its biggest military victories.

Aid agencies say their estimates are based on reports from local medical staff, displaced residents and relief workers, but acknowledge that conditions on the ground make precise figures hard to confirm.

The government has said it designated “safe zones” for civilians and has urged people to move into those areas. It has accused the LTTE of preventing civilians from leaving and using them as human shields, an allegation the rebels have denied. Humanitarian groups have expressed concern that shelling and fighting have continued near areas where civilians were told to seek refuge.

Mullaittivu has been one of the last major strongholds of the LTTE, which has fought for decades for an independent Tamil homeland in Sri Lanka’s north and east. The insurgency grew out of longstanding grievances among many Tamils over discrimination and political marginalization by the Sinhalese-majority state. The conflict has killed tens of thousands of people since it escalated into full-scale civil war in 1983.

The LTTE, also known as the Tamil Tigers, was once one of the world’s most powerful insurgent movements, operating a conventional fighting force, a naval wing and a network of suicide attackers. It has been designated a terrorist organization by several countries. The group has been accused of assassinations, suicide bombings, forced recruitment and using civilians as shields. Sri Lankan forces have also faced allegations from rights groups over civilian casualties, disappearances and abuses during the war.

As the army advances deeper into rebel-held territory, international agencies have called for greater protection of civilians, access for aid deliveries and safe passage for those seeking to leave the combat zone. The government says its offensive is aimed at ending the insurgency and restoring state control over the island.
